data.title: IMF tells RBA to stand ready for more hikes, even after 125bp of tightening this year
data.description:
The IMF's report adds institutional weight to the case against an early end to RBA tightening, which should keep markets wary of pricing in cuts soon. Short-dated Australian government bond yields are the most sensitive to that message. The IMF's explicit link to Middle East energy prices means oil is now a direct input into the RBA debate: a renewed spike in crude would strengthen the hawks' case. For the Australian dollar, a firmer rate outlook offers some support, but global risk sentiment and AI-related equity swings are likely to remain the bigger drivers. The December 8 decision and the next labour market data are the near-term tests.

---

data.title: Gold's downside looks limited because the dollar has already done most of its work, CBA says
data.description:
If CBA is right, gold traders should be watching the dollar index and US real yields more closely than geopolitical headlines. The December Fed decision is the near-term test. A hike that is already expected, with no hawkish surprise in the guidance, could let the dollar plateau and help gold stabilise. A signal that more hikes are coming would push real yields higher and test the lower end of CBA's range. Gold's renewed inverse link to the dollar also means moves in dollar-yen and euro-dollar may give an early read on bullion. With only weeks until year-end, CBA's range doubles as a near-term trading band.

---

data.title: Kiwi edges higher as official NZ election count confirms a hung parliament
data.description:
The muted reaction suggests NZD traders are pricing politics as noise unless talks break down. The tail risk is a failed negotiation and a fresh election, which would bring a longer period of uncertainty and could weigh on the currency and New Zealand government bonds. Coalition deals that come with large fiscal commitments are the other thing to watch, especially for bond yields. Outside Wellington, the kiwi remains tied to global risk sentiment and the US dollar. With the Fed widely expected to hike in December and AI-related volatility still unsettling equities, those forces are likely to outweigh the election result.

---

data.title: Tokyo core inflation hits 16-month high of 2.9%, firming the case for a December BoJ hike
data.description:
The data keeps a December hike as the base case, which should limit any yen weakness. With the yen near 160 per dollar, however, a 25 basis point move that is already widely expected may do little on its own. The bigger driver for the currency is likely to be any signal that the BoJ will speed up its pace of hikes, as board member Naoki Tamura has urged. Short-dated Japanese government bond yields remain sensitive to that guidance. Stock market instability tied to AI and chips is the main risk to the hike call, so a sharp drop in Japanese equities would quickly cut the odds of a December move.

---

data.title: HSBC flags $3,400 as gold's next big test and says it is too early to call a bottom
data.description:
Gold is trading as a risk asset rather than a haven, so equity markets have become the key driver. Another leg lower in stocks would raise the chance of a test of $3,400, while a stabilisation would ease the forced selling. Silver and platinum group metals face an extra layer of risk from tariffs that could hit the industries using them, even though HSBC still expects silver to be in deficit. US tariff announcements are worth watching, especially any aimed at Mexico or Canada, which HSBC sees as the exception that could lift silver. With the Fed widely expected to hike in December, a softer turn in US data is the most likely trigger for relief.

---

data.title: Australia's 12% investment surge, the biggest since 2011, keeps RBA hike risk alive: Citi
data.description:
A stronger-than-expected capex print pushes back against the view that the RBA has finished tightening, which should support short-dated Australian government bond yields. It could also give the Australian dollar some support through its rate advantage, though global risk sentiment is likely to remain the bigger driver for the currency. Markets will look to the GDP release, along with the next inflation and labour market data, to judge whether the investment surge is feeding through to prices. A weakening jobs market would argue for a hold, while sticky inflation would strengthen the case for another hike, leaving the RBA's next move closely balanced.

---

data.title: OCBC sees the Indian rupee strengthening to 92.10 per dollar by end-2027 as oil relief builds
data.description: For the rupee, oil is the swing factor. With OCBC keeping its end-2026 Brent forecast at $100 a barrel, any fresh attack on Gulf energy infrastructure or disruption around Hormuz could quickly reverse recent gains, since India imports most of its crude. The RBI's measures make one-way bets against the currency more expensive, which should limit sharp swings in USD/INR in either direction. A firm decision on India's inclusion in the Bloomberg Global Aggregate Index would be the clearest upside catalyst, as it would bring passive bond inflows. RBI reserve rebuilding means rupee strength is likely to be gradual, which suits carry trades more than outright momentum bets.

data.title: Goldman says hyperscalers can easily earn 15% on AI, but neoclouds face a utilisation trap
data.description:
The views point to a widening gap in how investors treat the AI trade. Hyperscaler stocks and investment-grade bonds look the most defensible, given their strong balance sheets and cash flows outside AI. Neocloud equity and high-yield credit carry the most risk if utilisation disappoints. Goldman's credit team expects the high-yield market for AI deals to split more sharply, with investors favouring top-tier developers and projects backed by solid contracts. Chipmakers and memory suppliers ultimately depend on the same thing as the neoclouds: evidence that companies using AI are earning a return. The next earnings round's commentary on returns on capital is likely to move the whole complex.

--

data.title: Gold's 37% slide from record looks overdone, says Saxo's Hansen, but $3,590 is the test
data.description:
Gold's moves are being set by the dollar and US rate pricing, not by safe-haven demand, so US data and Fed commentary will matter more than geopolitical headlines for any rebound. Because speculative positioning has been cut so hard, short covering could make any bounce sharp, especially in silver, the most stretched metal. A failure back below Wednesday's low would suggest forced selling has further to run. That would be a risk for miners and leveraged exposure. A softer dollar or a dovish shift in Fed expectations is the catalyst most likely to turn a technical rebound into a lasting one.

---

data.title: ECB picks Spain's Hernández de Cos as president, with 3 tests waiting from day one
data.description:
For bonds, the appointment matters most for the gap between French and German yields. Markets may treat a president who backed quantitative easing as a slightly firmer safety net for French debt, but his record on fiscal discipline makes a blanket rescue unlikely. That leaves French spreads tied to the election campaign more than to the ECB. The euro's immediate reaction is likely to be muted, since Hernández de Cos is seen as a continuity candidate, not someone who will change the direction of rates. Brunnermeier as chief economist is worth watching, as his academic work on financial stability could shape how the bank thinks about stepping into markets.

---

data.title: JPMorgan sees bitcoin capitulation in record Strategy discount, but 3 risks cloud the call
data.description:
For bitcoin, the June closing low near $58,500 is now the key level. A clean break would put the next on-chain support clusters, around $57,000 and then $47,000, in play, and would probably trigger more selling from miners whose costs sit well above the price. For Strategy shareholders, forced selling by index funds around the November 30 MSCI removal could widen the discount further before any rebound. Heavy options positioning could make moves in either direction more violent. A recovery in the ratio back above 1, as happened in July, would be the clearest sign that sellers are finished.

---

data.title: Five questions over Nvidia's China chip trail that Huang's return has not settled
data.description:
For Nvidia shareholders, the main risk is regulatory rather than personal. Tougher know-your-customer enforcement, or a revival of the push to require location tracking on chips, could slow shipments into Southeast Asia, which has been one of the company's biggest billing hubs. The stock already lost a large amount of market value during (well, prior to) the leadership crisis, so any new enforcement action or congressional hearing could hit sentiment quickly. Server makers such as Super Micro Computer are also exposed because of the pending prosecution. More broadly, the case adds to US-China tech tensions at a time when Washington's chip export policy is already in flux.

---

data.title: NZ consumer confidence breaks 100 as falling fuel prices cool inflation fears
data.description:
Households' inflation expectations have fallen sharply from their April peak, which eases one worry for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. That leans slightly against any hawkish shift in the policy outlook and is a mild negative for the New Zealand dollar at the margin. The survey's market impact is usually small, though, and moves in global risk appetite and the US dollar are likely to matter more for the currency. The main sensitivity to watch is oil: these readings now follow pump prices closely, so a renewed jump in crude would probably undo much of this month's improvement.

---

data.title: Tokyo CPI preview: core inflation seen jumping to 3% three weeks before BoJ decision
data.description:
A firm Tokyo print would add support for the yen, which is still trading near 160 per dollar despite close to $100 billion of intervention. The Fed is also hiking, so the rate gap stays wide, and a BoJ hike on its own may not change the yen's direction much without signs of a quicker pace afterwards. Short-dated Japanese government bond yields are the most exposed if the core-core measure meets or beats forecast. A miss would likely weigh on the yen and could revive talk of the BoJ pausing, especially if Nikkei weakness continues.

---

data.title: European stocks surge, S&P 500 futures finish higher in Thanksgiving trading
data.description:
The US Thanksgiving holiday didn't stand in the way of a strong day for global equities as European stock markets surged and S&P 500 futures closed up 38.75 points, or 0.54%.

The gains build on an impressive turnaround in US equities on Wednesday, when the Nasdaq erased much of an intraday decline of more than 4% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average recovered from a loss of more than 1,100 points to finish in positive territory.
